sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Floating-point numbers can be tricky! Let's learn how to avoid common numeric errors in loops and calculations.

• Why floating-point math can surprise you
• How to prevent tiny errors from adding up
• When to use integers instead of decimals

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you're cutting a pizza into thirds. You know each slice should be 0.333... of the pizza, but your knife can only cut to 0.33 or 0.333 accuracy. That tiny difference? That's a round-off error!

Computers have the same problem with floating-point numbers:
• They can't store infinite decimals (like 1/3)
• Small errors add up in loops
• Results might look wrong (like 0.5000000000000001 instead of 0.5)

The fix? Use integers when you can! For example:
• Count cents instead of dollars (100¢ = $1.00)
• Use whole numbers for precise counting

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ Floating-point numbers are approximations, not exact values
✓ Small errors add up in loops - be careful!
✓ Use integers for precise counting (like cents instead of dollars)
✓ Convert to decimal only at the end for display

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Multiply to work with integers (e.g., 100x for dollars → cents)
Compare floating-point numbers with a tolerance (e.g., `Math.abs(a-b) < 0.0001`)
donts: Don't use `==` to compare floating-point numbers
Don't add tiny decimals in loops (errors accumulate!)
sections.protip: For precise calculations, think in whole units (like cents) and convert only at the end!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is Minimizing Numeric Errors used in real apps?

examples.how: Store money as cents (integers) to avoid rounding errors in transactions
Use fixed-point math or tolerances to prevent tiny errors from breaking game logic
Special libraries handle precision for calculations like weather modeling

problem.description: Write a program that calculates the average of 3 temperatures (72.5, 81.2, 75.8) without floating-point errors. Hint: Convert to integers first!
hints: Multiply each temperature by 10 to work with integers
Divide by 10.0 at the end to get the decimal result
problem.explanation: By working with integers (725 instead of 72.5), we avoid floating-point errors. We divide by 3.0 (not 3) to force floating-point division, then by 10 to convert back to the original scale.

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Floating-point numbers are approximations - expect tiny errors
📌 Use integers for precise calculations (like cents instead of dollars)
📌 Convert to decimals only at the end for display
📌 Practice with real examples to spot these errors early!
